title: Postpartum Depression: Screening and Primary Care Management

evidenceAudit.scope: Woman in the first year after childbirth, seen in primary care, postnatal or well-baby clinic in Saudi Arabia: screening for postpartum depression, assessment of risk and suicidal thoughts, recognising postpartum psychosis, stepped treatment with self-help, psychological therapy and an antidepressant, and referral to a specialist perinatal mental health service. Uses NICE CG192 for the clinical pathway and a 2025 systematic review of Saudi studies for local prevalence and risk factors, with doses, administration and contraindications taken from product labels.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-20.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi Ministry of Health postpartum depression protocol was opened; the clinical pathway is NICE CG192 and the Saudi data are from a 2025 meta-analysis of 32 Saudi studies, so the authority is shown as Other.
NICE CG192 does not give doses; every dose, administration step and contraindication comes from the product label named in each row (US prescribing information).

Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) cut-offs vary in Saudi studies (10, 12, 13 and 14 were used) and the Saudi meta-analysis does not pick one; the cut-off to act on should be set with the local service. NICE CG192 does not set a cut-off.

Sertraline is chosen as the example antidepressant from the NICE advice to consider the woman's previous response and breastfeeding; NICE CG192 itself does not name sertraline, and it records uncertainty about safety in breastfeeding. The sertraline label reports low breast milk levels.
Zuranolone is a United States Food and Drug Administration approved drug for postpartum depression; its availability in Saudi Arabia was not verified and NICE CG192 pre-dates it.
The postpartum psychosis, bipolar disorder and infanticide-risk pathways are only mentioned as emergency referral points and are not written as treatment regimens.
Lithium, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines and mood stabilisers in the postnatal period (NICE CG192 Recommendations 1.4.18 to 1.4.37) are specialist prescribing and are not written as regimens.
Normal values for blood tests are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
Differentials follow standard clinical practice and were not drawn from one source section.
Figures were read through automated extraction of the NICE web text, open-access journal XML and DailyMed label XML; spot-check each dose against the source during clinical review.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register returned an empty page from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.

pathophysiology.summary: Postpartum depression is a depressive episode starting in the weeks after birth, with low mood, loss of interest, anxiety, sleep and appetite change, and trouble bonding or caring for the baby (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.3 and 1.6.1). Sudden changes in hormones, sleep loss, a history of depression and social stress combine to cause it; the Saudi review found the strongest links with limited family support, poor spouse support and unplanned pregnancy (Saudi PPD meta-analysis 2025, Results). In the 32 Saudi studies (10,975 women) the pooled prevalence depended on the screening cut-off: 18% at an Edinburgh scale score of 14 or more and 30% at 13 or more, with regional differences (Saudi PPD meta-analysis 2025, Results). Other risk factors reported in Saudi studies are the delivery method, young maternal age, and a personal or family history of depression (Saudi PPD meta-analysis 2025, Results). The illness is under-recognised because women may fear stigma or fear that their baby could be taken away, so they may not say how they feel (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.1 and 1.5.3). Untreated depression harms the mother and the mother-baby relationship; treatment follows severity, with psychological therapy or antidepressant for moderate to severe illness (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.8.1 to 1.8.3).

symptoms: Low mood, tearfulness, feeling hopeless or worthless most of the day for 2 weeks or more after delivery (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.4).
Loss of interest or pleasure, tiredness, poor concentration and sleep trouble beyond what the baby causes (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.4).
Anxiety, worry, panic, intrusive thoughts about the baby (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.3 and 1.5.6).
Difficulty bonding with or caring for the baby; thoughts of self-harm or of harming the baby (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.6.1 and 1.6.3).
physicalSigns: Flat or tearful affect, poor eye contact, slowed speech or agitation on interview (clinical judgment).
Poor self-care or poor attention to the baby; weight loss; looks unwell (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.6.3).
High EPDS or PHQ-9 score on screening (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.5).
redFlags: Suicidal thoughts or intent, or thoughts of harming the baby: same-day assessment by a mental health professional and make the baby safe (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.6.3).

Sudden onset of confusion, hallucinations, delusions, very elevated or very low mood, or not sleeping, usually in the first 2 weeks: suspect postpartum psychosis and refer for immediate assessment within 4 hours (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.11 and 1.5.12).

Any past or present severe mental illness, including bipolar disorder, or a first-degree relative with severe perinatal illness: refer to a specialist perinatal mental health service (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.9 and 1.5.10).
Domestic violence, child abuse or abandonment concerns: follow the safeguarding pathway (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.6.1 and 1.6.3).
Alcohol or drug misuse: assess and refer (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.13 and 1.5.14).
precipitants: Lack of social, family or spousal support (Saudi PPD meta-analysis 2025, Results).
Unplanned pregnancy; young maternal age; delivery method (Saudi PPD meta-analysis 2025, Results).
Personal or family history of depression or other mental illness (Saudi PPD meta-analysis 2025, Results; NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.9).
Domestic violence, trauma or childhood maltreatment; poor housing or economic stress (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.6.1).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Tearfulness and mood swings in the first week after birth that settle by about 2 weeks without treatment; PPD lasts longer and impairs function (clinical judgment).
Sudden onset in the first 2 weeks with confusion, hallucinations, delusions or a manic picture; an emergency needing assessment within 4 hours (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.12).
Past or family history of mania or hypomania; screen before starting any antidepressant (sertraline label, Section 2.3; NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.9).
Fatigue, mood change, palpitations or hair loss with abnormal thyroid function or low haemoglobin; check physical causes (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.6.1; clinical judgment).

differentials.condition: Anxiety disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder or post-traumatic stress after traumatic birth
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Prominent worry, intrusive thoughts or flashbacks; use the 2-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD-2) and GAD-7 (NICE CG192, Recommendations 1.5.4 to 1.5.7).
Tiredness that improves when sleep is protected, with intact mood and interest (clinical judgment).

ruleIn.testName: Two depression identification questions plus the 2-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD-2)
ruleIn.targetCondition: Depression and anxiety in the postnatal period
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Positive answer to either depression question; GAD-2 score of 3 or more
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Ask at first primary care contact and in the early postnatal period; a positive answer prompts a full assessment (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.4 to 1.5.6).
ruleIn.normalValue: Negative on both questions and GAD-2 score below 3

clinicalManagement.title: Ask and screen
clinicalManagement.timeframe: First contact in primary care and the early postnatal period
actions: Ask the two depression identification questions and the 2-item anxiety scale in a general talk about her wellbeing (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.4).
If positive, or you are worried, use the EPDS or PHQ-9 as part of a full assessment, or refer to the GP or a mental health professional (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.5).
Repeat the questions and a scale at all later contacts in the first year (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.8).
Create a safe space: women may fear stigma or fear losing the baby (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.1).

clinicalManagement.title: Assess and make a risk plan
actions: Take the history: past mental illness, treatment and response, physical health, sleep, alcohol and drugs, attitude to the baby, support, partner, housing and violence (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.6.1).
Do a risk assessment for self-harm, suicide, self-neglect and harm to the baby with the woman and, if she agrees, her family (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.6.3).
Ask about past severe mental illness or severe perinatal illness in a first-degree relative (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.9).
Check thyroid and haemoglobin to exclude physical causes (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.6.1).

clinicalManagement.title: Act on emergencies
actions: Sudden confusion, hallucinations, delusions or manic symptoms in the first 2 weeks: refer to a specialist perinatal mental health service for assessment within 4 hours (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.12).
Any severe mental illness, suspected or past: refer to a secondary or perinatal mental health service (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.10).
Suicidal intent or risk to the baby: do not leave her alone, arrange urgent mental health assessment and safeguard the baby (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.6.3).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat mild symptoms
actions: Offer facilitated self-help for persistent subthreshold symptoms or mild to moderate depression (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.8.1).
Give information on sleep, support, activity and practical help; involve family with her consent (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.6.1).
Review in 2 to 4 weeks with the same scale; step up if no improvement (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.8).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat moderate to severe depression
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Assess within 2 weeks of referral; therapy within 1 month
actions: Offer high-intensity psychological therapy such as cognitive behavioural therapy (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.8.3).

Offer an antidepressant if she prefers medication, declines therapy or has not responded, after discussing the risks of the drug and of untreated illness; sertraline is the example in this topic (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.8.3).
Combine therapy and medication if the response to either alone is poor (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.8.3).
A woman with a history of severe depression who has mild symptoms may be offered an antidepressant (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.8.2).
Discuss breastfeeding before prescribing; explain benefits, uncertainty about safety and the risk of stopping an effective drug (NICE CG192, Recommendations 1.4.4 and 1.4.17).
Screen for bipolar disorder before starting an antidepressant and agree how symptoms will be monitored with a scale (sertraline label, Section 2.3; NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.4.9).

clinicalManagement.title: Monitor and step up
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Weekly at first, then each visit
actions: Review response, side effects and risk at 1 to 2 weeks after starting a drug, then at each contact; repeat the scale (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.4.9 and 1.5.8).
If there is no response, refer to a specialist perinatal service for advice, including drugs such as zuranolone if available (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.4.5).
Do not stop a helpful antidepressant abruptly; reduce gradually (sertraline label, Section 2.6).
Share information about past and present mental health with the maternity service and health visitor (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.2).

regimens.indication: Moderate to severe postpartum depression (the label indication is major depressive disorder)
regimens.patientGroup: Postnatal women, including those who are breastfeeding
regimens.dose: Start 50 mg once daily; increase by 25 mg to 50 mg once a week according to response and tolerability; therapeutic range 50 mg to 200 mg a day, maximum 200 mg a day. Dilution and preparation: none; oral dose form, no reconstitution.
regimens.route: Oral, once daily at the same time each day (sertraline label, Section 2.1)
regimens.duration: Continue for a number of months after recovery; stop slowly, never abruptly (sertraline label, Section 2.6)
adjustments: Hepatic: mild impairment (Child-Pugh 5 or 6) needs half the usual dose; moderate or severe impairment is not recommended (sertraline label, Section 2.4).

Breastfeeding: sertraline and its metabolites are in breast milk at low levels; breastfed infants had about 2% of the mother's serum level with no adverse reactions in a pooled analysis of 53 pairs (sertraline label, Section 8.2); NICE CG192 records uncertainty about safety (Recommendation 1.4.17).
Switching from an MAOI: wait at least 14 days (sertraline label, Section 2.5).
Antidepressants in late pregnancy carry a small increased risk of postpartum haemorrhage and neonatal adaptation syndrome; relevant if she is pregnant again (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.4.16).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register returned an empty page from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Depression score (EPDS or PHQ-9) and suicidal thoughts at 1 to 2 weeks, then each visit; watch for early worsening and agitation (sertraline label, Section 5.1).
Serotonin syndrome signs, bleeding, low sodium and, in breastfed babies, feeding, sleep and weight (sertraline label, Section 5; NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.4.17).
contraindications: Taking or within 14 days of stopping an MAOI, including linezolid and intravenous methylene blue (sertraline label, Section 4).
Known hypersensitivity to sertraline, such as anaphylaxis or angioedema (sertraline label, Section 4).
regimens.branch: Moderate or severe postpartum depression: first-line antidepressant
regimens.sourceTitle: NICE CG192: Antenatal and postnatal mental health: clinical management and service guidance
regimens.sourceEdition: NICE CG192 Recommendation 1.8.3 and Recommendation 1.4.17; sertraline hydrochloride tablets US label, Section 2.1 to Section 2.6, Section 4 and Section 8.2

regimens.patientGroup: Postnatal adults with severe depression under a perinatal mental health service
regimens.dose: 50 mg once daily in the evening for 14 days (a total made from the labelled capsule strengths); reduce to 40 mg if central nervous system depressant effects occur; 30 mg with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C) or eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m2. Dilution and preparation: none; oral dose form, no reconstitution.
regimens.route: Oral capsules, swallowed whole with fat-containing food (400 to 1,000 calories, 25% to 50% fat) in the evening (Zurzuvae label, Section 2.1)
regimens.duration: 14 days; use beyond 14 days is not established (Zurzuvae label, Section 2.1)
adjustments: Avoid with CYP3A4 inducers (Zurzuvae label, Section 2.2).
Do not take a double dose after a missed evening dose; continue the course (Zurzuvae label, Section 2.5).
Can be used alone or with an oral antidepressant (Zurzuvae label, Section 2.1).
Advise effective contraception during treatment and for 1 week after the last dose (Zurzuvae label, Section 5.4).
Breastfeeding: low levels in milk; weigh benefit and risk (Zurzuvae label, Section 8.2).
Availability in Saudi Arabia not verified; specialist decision.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register returned an empty page from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Sedation and driving: boxed warning; no driving or hazardous tasks until at least 12 hours after each dose throughout the 14-day course (Zurzuvae label, Boxed Warning).
Mood and suicidal thoughts during treatment (Zurzuvae label, Section 5.3).
Drowsiness in breastfed infants if breastfeeding (clinical judgment).
contraindications: The label lists no contraindication (Zurzuvae label, Section 4: None).
Boxed warning: impaired ability to drive or do hazardous activities (Zurzuvae label).

branches.entryCriteria: Postnatal woman with moderate or severe depression who prefers medication, declines or has not responded to psychological therapy, with no bipolar disorder, no psychosis, no MAOI or pimozide use and a plan for monitoring; breastfeeding discussed.

branches.entryCriteria: Postnatal adult with severe postpartum depression under a specialist perinatal mental health service, when the drug is available locally and driving can be avoided; negative pregnancy test and effective contraception.

medicationPlan.note: Drug class and indication follow NICE CG192; doses, administration and contraindications come from the US prescribing information named in each row. All doses are for adults. NICE CG192 notes that use of tricyclic antidepressants, SSRIs and (S)NRIs in pregnancy and the postnatal period was off-label when the guideline was written (Recommendation 1.4.16). SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register returned an empty page from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Screening questions at the first contact and early postnatal period
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Two depression identification questions (feeling down, depressed or hopeless; little interest or pleasure) and the 2-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale; positive answer or clinical concern leads to the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale or Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) (NICE CG192, Recommendations 1.5.4 and 1.5.5).
At all later contacts in the first postnatal year consider the two questions, the 2-item scale and EPDS or PHQ-9 for monitoring (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.8).
GAD-2 score of 3 or more: use GAD-7 or refer (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.5.6).

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale cut-offs in Saudi studies
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Scores of 10, 12, 13 and 14 or more have been used; prevalence was 45% at 10, 30% at 13 and 18% at 14 or more, so the cut-off must be agreed locally (Saudi PPD meta-analysis 2025, Results).

High-intensity psychological therapy (such as cognitive behavioural therapy), or an antidepressant if she prefers medication, declines therapy or has not responded; combine if response is poor (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.8.3).
Assess within 2 weeks of referral and give psychological therapy within 1 month of assessment (NICE CG192, Recommendation 1.7.3).

values: No single drug is named; choose by previous response, pregnancy stage and breastfeeding (Recommendations 1.4.16 and 1.4.17)
Sertraline is labelled for major depression; zuranolone is labelled for postpartum depression in adults
Uncertainty about safety; seek specialist advice (Recommendation 1.4.17)
Low levels in milk; sertraline infants had about 2% of maternal serum level (sertraline label, Section 8.2)
No fixed score; use a scale as part of full assessment (Recommendation 1.5.5)
Not applicable (labels do not set screening thresholds)

teaching.scope: Woman in the first year after childbirth, seen in primary care, postnatal or well-baby clinic in Saudi Arabia: screening for postpartum depression, assessment of risk and suicidal thoughts, recognising postpartum psychosis, stepped treatment with self-help, psychological therapy and an antidepressant, and referral to a specialist perinatal mental health service. Uses NICE CG192 for the clinical pathway and a 2025 systematic review of Saudi studies for local prevalence and risk factors, with doses, administration and contraindications taken from product labels.
learningObjectives: Screen every woman in the first postnatal year with two questions and a scale.
Assess risk of suicide, harm to the baby and psychosis at every contact.
Treat by severity: self-help, psychological therapy, then an antidepressant.
Refer urgently for psychosis or severe illness.
pitfalls: Dismissing low mood as baby blues beyond two weeks.
Treating postpartum psychosis in primary care.
Starting an antidepressant without asking about mania.
Stopping breastfeeding by default without discussing risks and benefits.
Missing partner and family support needs.
keyPoints: Postpartum psychosis is an emergency needing assessment within 4 hours.
Screen for bipolar disorder before starting an antidepressant.
Do not stop an antidepressant abruptly.
Zuranolone causes drowsiness: no driving for 12 hours after each dose.
Screening cut-offs differ in Saudi studies and must be set locally.

patientEducation: Postpartum depression is common and treatable; it is not your fault and does not mean you are a bad mother.
Tell us if you have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby; we will help you straight away.
Take your medicine every day; do not stop suddenly.
Ask a trusted family member to help with night feeds so you can sleep.
You can still breastfeed on some medicines; we will discuss the choices.
lifestyleAndDiet: Eat regular meals and take short walks.
Avoid alcohol while unwell and on medicine.
Keep in contact with family and friends.
mdtReferrals: Primary care physician; health visitor or community midwife; obstetrician; psychologist for cognitive behavioural therapy; perinatal psychiatrist; social worker; paediatrician for the infant; clinical pharmacist for lactation advice.
dischargeCriteria: Screen negative or improving, risk assessment recorded, treatment plan agreed, safety plan and contacts given, family informed with consent, and follow-up booked.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review at 1 to 2 weeks after a drug is started, then every 2 to 4 weeks until recovered; repeat the screening scale at all contacts during the first postnatal year; refer to specialist services if there is no response or risk increases; continue an effective antidepressant for several months after recovery and stop gradually.
